title: Bartz v. Anthropic — order on fair use: training on lawfully acquired books is fair use; pirated-library copying is not
pub: N.D. Cal., Order on Fair Use (ECF No. 231)
author: William Alsup

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses copyright fair use for distinct stages of LLM development and data handling, not AI’s task-level capabilities, human verification, selective deployment or legal-work redesign. Its use-specific analysis is conceptually analogous to context-specific evaluation but does not establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.

It therefore directly supports product-purpose and market-specific analysis rather than categorical treatment of AI training.

kp.k: Training and library acquisition require separate fair-use analysis
kp.d: Judge William Alsup distinguishes copying to train particular LLMs from acquiring and retaining a permanent, general-purpose library. The order grants Anthropic summary judgment on training and on destructive digitization of purchased books, but rejects treating pirated library acquisitions as protected training copies. The decision evaluates particular uses rather than granting an AI-specific exemption.

kp.k: Training was transformative despite copying protected expression
kp.d: The court holds that training Claude’s underlying LLMs to generate new text was transformative, even accepting the authors’ position that training selected their creative expression and compressed or memorized their works. Factors one, three and four favored training; the expressive nature of the books weighed against fair use. Memorization was assumed for this motion, not established as an independent technical finding.

kp.d: The court accepts that Anthropic could have trained without these particular books, or without books altogether, but finds the copying reasonably necessary given training’s scale and the benefits of strong writing examples. kp.k: Competition and training licensing did not defeat fair use
kp.d: The authors argued that AI would produce an explosion of competing writing and displace an emerging training-licensing market. The court assumes those possibilities in the authors’ favor rather than finding their magnitude empirically. It nevertheless concludes that competition from noninfringing new works is not the substitution copyright protects against, and that the authors cannot control a licensing market for this fair training use.

kp.k: Destructive digitization of purchased books was independently fair
kp.d: Anthropic purchased millions of print books and scanned them while discarding the originals. The court separately approves this one-for-one replacement for storage and searchability, emphasizing that the replacement copies remained internal rather than being redistributed. Factors one and three favored fair use, factor two slightly opposed it, and factor four was neutral. This is a fact-specific format-conversion holding, not approval of unrestricted duplication or sharing.

kp.k: Pirated permanent libraries remained outside the training justification
kp.d: The order describes downloads from Books3, LibGen and PiLiMi totaling over seven million book copies, retained even when not selected for training or no longer needed for it. All four factors weighed against this library use: it substituted unpaid copies for purchasable books. cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge William Alsup distinguishes transformative LLM training from acquiring a permanent pirated library, while addressing AI’s effects on writing competition and training-data markets.
pts.d: This is principally a cross-domain source concerning AI development, books and copyright, rather than a forecast about legal employment. Alsup holds that Anthropic’s use of books to train LLMs was fair use on this record, separately from its initial acquisition of library copies. He also holds that destructive digitization of purchased print books for internal storage and searchability was fair use on the specified facts. He rejects fair-use justification for acquiring and retaining pirated books as a permanent, general-purpose library; later training does not excuse that separate use. On competition, he accepts for purposes of the motion the authors’ contention that LLMs could generate an explosion of competing writing, but concludes that competition without infringing reproduction is not the displacement copyright protects against. He similarly assumes a training-licensing market could develop but concludes that authors cannot control the particular training use held fair here. The order reports Anthropic’s belief that books were a cost-effective route to high-quality LLMs, rather than independently establishing comparative training economics. Its specific legal-services analogy distinguishes a competing legal-opinion retrieval tool in Thomson Reuters v. Ross from a hypothetical generative tool producing fresh legal writing; it does not predict lawyer replacement or quantify legal-service productivity.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on a summary-judgment record and copyright doctrine, not on independent AI benchmarks or measured labour-market outcomes.
pts.d: Alsup applies the four factors of Section 107 using party submissions, internal Anthropic communications, deposition testimony, discovery responses and expert reports. The record describes downloads from Books3, LibGen and PiLiMi during 2021–2022; millions of purchased print books subsequently scanned destructively; retention of a general-purpose library; selection of subsets for training; and input/output filtering around public-facing Claude. The legal reasoning draws on Warhol, Google Books, HathiTrust, Texaco, Sega, Sony and other copyright decisions. The legal-research comparison draws on Thomson Reuters v. Ross and Alsup’s analogy to White v. West Publishing. Alleged memorization within trained models is accepted for purposes of the motion, not independently resolved. The authors’ predictions about competing works and possible licensing markets are likewise assumed in their favour, rather than presented as demonstrated market outcomes. There are no benchmark results establishing legal-writing accuracy, lawyer productivity or displacement.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The June 23, 2025 order is fact-specific and procedural; future market effects have no quantified horizon.
pts.d: The holdings concern conduct examined in this June 23, 2025 district-court order. Anthropic began acquiring pirated books in 2021, released Claude publicly in March 2023 and pursued bulk print acquisition and scanning in 2024. Training fair use is assessed on a record with no allegation that infringing outputs of the authors’ works reached Claude users. The court leaves open a different action if infringing outputs emerge. The digitization holding concerns one-for-one replacement of purchased print copies, destruction of originals and no external redistribution—not a general permission to multiply or distribute digital books. The denial concerning pirated library copies leaves a trial on those copies and resulting damages, including willfulness; subsequent purchases do not erase the earlier conduct, though they may affect statutory damages. Other copying for non-training uses is not resolved because the record is insufficiently developed. The court’s broader skepticism about piracy even when followed immediately by transformative use is expressly unnecessary to deciding these facts. No date or scale is specified for an increase in competing writing or development of training-licensing markets.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are Anthropic, authors and book rightsholders; implications for legal-AI providers are illustrative rather than measured.
pts.d: Anthropic obtains a favourable ruling on training and specified print-to-digital conversion but remains exposed concerning pirated-library copying and damages. The named authors—Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber and Kirk Wallace Johnson—and their affiliated rightsholding entities cannot recover on the training theory rejected here, but retain claims concerning pirated acquisition and potentially other copying or future infringing outputs. More broadly, authors and publishers may face competition from AI-assisted writing and limits on charging for uses classified as fair, while retaining protection against acquisition that substitutes for paid copies. Claude users, including less capable writers and paying corporate clients, are described as obtaining text-generation assistance; the order does not establish its quality through independent testing. Legal-information publishers and legal-AI developers appear through the contrast between competing retrieval and generative legal writing. No specific effects on law-firm staffing, fees, in-house departments or access to justice are established.
